title: Swidden in Plain Sight
bodyHtml:
Kri is a Vietic language spoken in Laos, with about 250 speakers as of 2009. Below are some words in Kri, alongside their English translations. Kri vowels come in two registers, heavy and light, but for simplicity this distinction is not marked in this problem.

blang
(of the eyes) to become open1
balang
to open one's eyes
plaajh
an arm span2
palaajh
to measure something by arm spans
cabuuc
to pick up or measure out purse-hand3
truum
to be on its face
paang
to signal ownership of a swidden4
ckaang
a hand span5
basơt
to turn off, put out
kooq
to live
bsơt
to go out (as a light or fire does)
cakaang
to measure something by hand spans
cooh
to pierce
krnooq
a house
prnaang
a sign placed in a swidden to show ownership

1 As an example, this verb can be used to describe the point a few weeks into a puppy's life, when its eyes open for the first time.
2 An arm span is the length of a person's outstretched arms, from fingertips to fingertips.
3 Purse-hand means to put the thumb and other four fingers together in a pinching motion.
4 A swidden is an agricultural field that has been cleared by cutting and burning vegetation.
5 A hand span is the length of a person's hand.

B1. Give the Kri word for each of the following:

  1. a unit of measure equal to an amount that can be picked up purse-hand
  2. to put something on its face
  3. a hanging thread, pierced through many objects

Here are six more Kri words. Their English meanings are given below, in a random order.

A. kaleer    B. kleer    C. koorq    D. krneep    E. krnoorq    F. paraang

  1. to scoop out strips of a vegetable for food preparation
  2. to fall off (as a fruit does)
  3. an instrument to scoop out strips of a vegetable
  4. to take someone across (e.g., across a river)
  5. tongs, pincers
  6. to pick something off (e.g., to pick a berry off of a bush)

B2. Match the Kri words (A to F) with their English translations (1 to 6).

B3. A Kri word in this problem can be modified to translate exactly one of the English phrases below. Choose that phrase and give the Kri word that translates it.

  1. a river
  2. to put someone into a river
  3. to cross over
  4. a cross

hints.text: Line up the words that clearly belong together in pairs or triples, for example plaajh / palaajh and kooq / krnooq. In each set, the consonants and vowels of the 'core' of the word stay the same, and something extra gets added inside the word, not at the beginning or end.

Kri uses infixes: extra material slipped in right after the very first consonant. One infix builds an action verb (doing something, or making something happen) out of a noun or a state; the other infix builds a noun (an instrument, a physical thing, or the result of the action) out of a verb. Decide which infix is which, then remember that you can also work backwards: strip an infix off to recover the simpler base word.

Practice on a pair that is not asked about: blang means '(of the eyes) to become open', and balang means 'to open one's eyes'. So inserting -a- after the first consonant b turns the plain happening into something an agent does. Check the same insertion in bsơt 'to go out', so basơt 'to turn off, put out'. Now find the other infix by comparing kooq 'to live' with krnooq 'a house'.

explanationHtml:
What to notice first

Kri words in this problem come in families. Members of a family share the same skeleton of consonants and vowels, and differ only by something inserted inside the word, just after the first consonant. Linguists call such an inserted piece an infix (English mostly uses prefixes and suffixes, like un- and -ness, so infixes feel unusual to us).

Two families to compare:

  • plaajh 'an arm span' vs. palaajh 'to measure something by arm spans'
  • kooq 'to live' vs. krnooq 'a house'

In the first, -a- is slipped in after p. In the second, -rn- is slipped in after k.

Infix 1: -a- makes an action verb

Collect all the -a- pairs:

  • blang '(of the eyes) to become open' gives balang 'to open one's eyes' (someone makes it happen)
  • bsơt 'to go out (of a fire)' gives basơt 'to put out' (someone makes it happen)
  • plaajh 'an arm span' (a unit) gives palaajh 'to measure by arm spans' (use the unit)
  • ckaang 'a hand span' gives cakaang 'to measure by hand spans'

So -a- takes a state or a thing and gives you a verb meaning 'do it / cause it / use it'. Notice that -a- only appears in words whose base begins with two consonants (bl-, bs-, pl-, ck-): the infix breaks up that cluster.

Infix 2: -rn- makes a noun

  • kooq 'to live' gives krnooq 'a house' (the place/thing for living)
  • paang 'to signal ownership of a swidden' gives prnaang 'a sign placed in a swidden to show ownership' (the physical thing used)

So -rn- turns a verb into a concrete noun: the instrument, object, or result of the action.

Working backwards

The key trick is that the rules run in both directions. cabuuc 'to pick up or measure out purse-hand' already contains the verb-making -a-. Peel it off and you get the base noun cbuuc, which must be the unit of measure — exactly parallel to ckaang / cakaang. That solves B1a.

For B1b, truum 'to be on its face' is a state, and we want the caused version 'to put something on its face'. Insert -a- after the first consonant t: taruum.

For B1c, cooh 'to pierce' is a verb, and 'a hanging thread pierced through many objects' is a physical thing produced by piercing — a noun. Insert -rn- after c: crnooh.

B2: sorting the six new words

Look at the shapes:

  • koorq — plain verb, so 'to scoop out strips of a vegetable' (1)
  • krnoorq — the -rn- noun of that verb, so 'an instrument to scoop out strips' (3)
  • kleer — plain verb with a cluster, a spontaneous happening, so 'to fall off (as a fruit does)' (2)
  • kaleer — the -a- version of kleer, caused by someone, so 'to pick something off' (6)
  • krneep — contains -rn-, so it is an instrument noun, so 'tongs, pincers' (5)
  • paraang — contains -a- after p, so a caused verb, so 'to take someone across' (4)

Note how the caused/spontaneous pair kleer / kaleer matches blang / balang: the fruit falling by itself vs. a person picking it off.

B3: which phrase is buildable?

We need a word in the problem that can be modified to fit one phrase. Start from paraang 'to take someone across'. Since -a- is the causing infix, its base must be praang, and the base of a caused verb is the plain happening: 'to cross over' — phrase 9. So the answer is 9, praang.

Why not the others? 'A river' and 'a cross' are nouns, but the -rn- infix makes instruments and results of an action, not the setting or the shape, and neither 'river' nor 'cross' is the thing produced by crossing. 'To put someone into a river' is a different caused meaning that no single infix on any given word delivers. Only 'to cross over' falls out of the system directly.
